content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper analyses the properties of threshold functions for generating solutions of optimization problems formulated using mixed-integer programming. These functions have been used in prior work upon which this paper is based on. In addition to results on such functions, the authors also claim better results than prior work using recently proposed benchmarks from a NeurIPS competition.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Although I love seeing work on MIP in machine learning conferences, my reaction to this paper is mostly negative for the following reasons:
- In general, the theoretical results explore very little the structure of MIP problems, to the point that many of these results have nothing to do with the main object of the paper (MIP).
- The existence of a threshold function for feasibility (constrained by objective function or not) given the assignment of variables based on a score (whatever that score is) is obvious: you are basically sorting the variables in some order and every assignment reduces the probability of a solution being feasible. 
- The paper is heavy on notation and short on intuition: if there is not enough space to even state the results used (such as Theorem 3), I do not see the point of spending so much time in definitions; I would encourage the authors to rewrite this work to discuss the ideas in the paper and the theory in the appendix, as several authors have successfully done in papers published in machine learning conferences. In fact, this is main issue with this paper: I spent a lot of time trying to understand the value of the theoretical developments, and I am still not certain that they are significant enough.
- The methodological part is in greater part a small improvement of an existing technique. For example, it is difficult to read Section 3 without prior knowledge of the topic.
- The entirety of the computational results is reported in a heavily compressed table (nothing more in the appendix) and they deal with very specific and short time limits. The convention in the MIP literature is to use performance profile plots to show many problems are cumulatively solved up to the time limit thanks to a new technique, and then the plot continues with the gap obtained for the problems that were not solved to optimality. It is very difficult to judge an algorithm based on a such a limited picture of the results.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
In addition to my points above, I would encourage the authors to rewrite this paper with a focus on the problem that they are trying to solve; and then bring the technical elements as needed, with the appropriate background described, and contextualizing their need before delving into technicalities. I would also recommend that the authors follow more closely the notation and terminology used in MIP; you can find more specific comments about that below.

Abstract:
- "MIP solver is integrated into the end-to-end learning framework.": please rewrite

Intro:
- "We propose a simple heuristic of setting a confidence threshold hyperparameter, and selecting all variables of which the confidence score is above this threshold.": at this point, if a reader has never seen prior work, it is not possible to understand this.

Section 2:
- The fact that some decision variables are integer and others are continuous should be part of the constraints; the bounds are much less relevant
- "when x satisfies the linear constraint": constraints?
- "be the lower and upper variable": bound instead of variable? 
- "otherwise not fixed": rewrite

Section 3:
- Hard to follow without knowing prior work.

Section 4:
- "of partial variables" [used multiple times]: do you mean "of partial assignments"?
- The notation around equation (8) is unnecessarily complex
- Theorem 3 should be explained when mentioned in Page 5
- "LP-relaxation objective satisfiability": Feasibility of LP-relaxation with bounded objective?
- "have a lower bound of quality": rewrite
content.summary_of_the_review: I am not seeing an intuitive contribution on the theory or a comprehensive evaluation of the experiments that would justify this paper being accepted. It is possible that there is something great and meaningful in this work, but I believe the paper should be rewritten to show that.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tries to build a theoretical foundation for their post-hoc method for choosing the selection rate when solving MIP problems.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The authors tried to justify their method with some theoretical analysis.

Weakness:

1. The theorems given in the paper are really hard to understand. I suggest the authors simplify their notations and also give more insights and intuitions of their theorems.

2. Do the authors improve the method which won the second place of ML4CO? If they improved, I think it is better to compare with the top 2 methods in that competition. In addition, the author should more clearly point out the improvements they have made based on their theoretical foundations. If the method is the same, then the major contributions are the theoretical foundations which are not quite clear to me. I hope the theoretical foundation can guide the community to improve neural diving methods.

3. There are a lot of typos in the paper, especially in the theorem sections. For example, "Proposition 1" is introduced on Page 8 but the authors started referring to it on Page 7. I think "Proposition 1" on Page 7 should be "Theorem 1". This kind of typo really makes me hard to understand their theoretical contributions.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing of the paper should be significantly improved. The current version is hard to follow, which makes the authors' claims hard to justify.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this is a paper that tries to tackle an interesting problem from a theoretical point of view. However, I don't think it convinces me their contributions can be justified.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Neural diving is a learning-based approach for finding high quality feasible solutions to a combinatorial optimization problem, which has a crucial parameter called coverage. This paper showed the existence of threshold functions in learning to generate feasible solutions of MIP, and further proposed a post-hoc method and a learning-based approach that enables more efficient coverage optimization. The numerical experiments demonstrate that the method in this paper outperforms the compared benchmark methods in various datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: As part of the exciting trend of incorporating learning techniques in combinatorial optimization problems or MIPs, this paper made an impressive advancement over the Neural diving approach proposed in another recent paper, by theoretically showing that there exist threshold functions in feasibility and feasible optimality over the selection rate. The authors also proposed a Post-hoc Confidence Thresholding which improves the training inefficiency of SelectiveNet in Neural diving. As far as I'm concerned, the theory of this paper is correct and the numerical experiments are convincing. 

Weakness: The numerical experiment setup can be introduced in a more detailed fashion. For example, where does the performance of CT and TaL stand when compared with the methods on the leaderboard of ML4CO competition. Also, the authors claimed "for set covering, ..., we solve the problems for 1, 10, and 5 seconds, respectively", then why Table 1 does not have 0 OG?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Even though I had a hard time following some of the theory details, but I think overall this paper is very nicely written and structured clearly. As far as I can see, the results in this paper are novel and correct.
content.summary_of_the_review: Finding feasible solution with good objective value to a combinatorial optimization problem is a very important and challenging task. Based on the contribution of this paper to the community of ML4CO, I believe that it is a high-quality paper that can be accepted into top conference like ICLR.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: We appreciate your reviews.
content.comment:
We withdraw this submission to revise our overall manuscript based on the reviewers' points.

We have indeed improved the method that won second place in ML4CO. Comparing our improved method with the top-2 methods in the competition is reasonable, but the winner's method is not learning-based; they used the traditional solver-tuning approach [1]. Since they have yet to release the details on the parameters they tuned, it is not feasible for us to reproduce their result.

In this manuscript, we focused on linking the theory of threshold functions with the learning-based generative model to solve MIP problems. In this regard, we intended to formulate our theory and learning algorithm to encompass general MIP class structures. Since we build on the learning-based model, the threshold function values depend not only on the structure of MIP problems but also on the training dataset distribution and neural network training settings. This high degree of freedom is the motivation of our method to learn the threshold function. The importance of the threshold function in learning to generate feasible MIP solutions is in its scalability. The threshold function is a surrogate measure of a neural net model's performance in generating feasible MIP solutions in scalable settings.

Our theoretical result does not assume any  specific ordering of variables; our result deals with the random subset, where the probability distribution of a variable selection is uniformly random, which is more general. 

We appreciate the reviewers' comments on our writing.

[1] Gasse, Maxime, et al. "The machine learning for combinatorial optimization competition (ml4co): Results and insights." NeurIPS 2021 Competitions and Demonstrations Track . PMLR, 2022.
